Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable comments. We have revised the manuscript to clarify these issues.
1. In the Introduction section, the authors claimed that the TPD systems based on peptides or aptamers have limited tissue persistence. However, it seems that the HFn-LYTAC has very short half-life and not very promising tumor tissue accumulation. It is hard to see the advantages of this system compared with the recent published work of TransTAC and Pep-TAC.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point, which allows us to critically reflect on the research significance of our manuscript.
A previous study developed an LYTAC based on a TfR1-targeting peptide and a PD-L1 antibody-derived scFv fragment (TfR-LYTAC). However, its short plasma half-life limits tissue persistence. Administering TfR-LYTAC alone fails to effectively suppress tumors, and an additional delivery system is needed to improve therapeutic efficacy (Ref 1). This highlights the limited tissue persistence of peptide-based LYTACs. Although a direct comparison of plasma half-lives between HFn-LYTAC and TfR-LYTAC is not feasible (no relevant data are available for TfR-LYTAC), our results demonstrate that HFn6-PEP has a significantly HER2 extended plasma half-life compared with that of the free HER2-targeting protein PEP (20.2 HER2 kDa), with a 14-fold increase (131.8 min for HFn6-PEP and 9.3 min for PEP ) (Only HER2 HER2 for reviewer Fig. 1). Given that the shedding of fluorescent groups could interfere with the accurate characterization of HFn-LYTAC, we further utilized Western blotting to directly evaluate its in vivo behavior and accordingly updated the original dataset. Western blotting analysis further confirmed that HFn6-PEP has a half-life of ~227 min (Fig. 5a). In vivo HER2 distribution studies revealed that HFn6-PEP preferentially accumulated at the tumor site, HER2 with levels 10–16 times greater than those in major normal organs (Fig. 5b, c).
The half-life of HFn-LYTAC is shorter than that of TransTAC (16.6 days); however, increasing the dosing frequency allows HFn-LTYAC to achieve comparable POI degradation efficiency in vivo. Moreover, subsequent supplementary experiments suggest that rapid uptake by monocytes may contribute to the shortened circulation time (Supplementary Fig. 6a), providing a direction for future optimization.
Compared with the two works mentioned by the reviewers, the feature of this study lies in the introduction of a plug-and-play modular LYTAC platform. The scaffold and POI ligands are designed separately, enabling easy large-scale preparation and modular assembly. The HFn6 scaffold serves as a universal platform, allowing LYTAC construction by simple incubation and conjugation with the target POI ligand—without additional chemical modifications, as required in Pep-TAC, which is based on peptides.

5. The enhanced affinity of HFn6 for TfR1 via mutagenesis is a key innovation. However, the rationale for selecting specific residues (D15, F81, Q83, N109, K119, D123) in the TfR1-binding interface remains unclear. Please explicitly justify the selection of these residues (e.g., structural analysis, computational predictions, or prior literature). In Extended Data Fig. 1b, include computational data (e.g., binding free energy changes, hydrogen bond/electrostatic interactions) for each mutation. In Fig. 1b (mislabeled as Fig. 1c in the text), highlight the N109R and K119R mutation sites in the molecular docking interface, annotate bond energies, and provide the PDB ID of the HFn-TfR1 complex in the figure legend or Methods. Simplify Extended Data Fig. 1a: Use a single panel with “front view”; and “rotated 180° view”; to illustrate the overall binding mode, labeling key interacting residues.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and suggestions. The selection of HFn mutation sites was based on the analysis of the structure of the HFn and TfR1 ectodomain complex. The N-terminal and BC loop regions of HFn interact with the apical domain of TfR1 (Fig. 2a, b). The structural reorganization caused by complex formation is limited to the side chains that are in direct contact with amino acids, resulting in a relatively low affinity between the two. Therefore, it is theoretically possible to increase the affinity of HFn for TfR1 by strengthening the interaction between the side chains of amino acids at the binding interface of HFn and TfR1 or by introducing more amino acid residues involved in the interaction. Consequently, residues D15, F81, Q83, N109, K119 and D123, which are located in the vicinity of the interaction region and have no or limited interactions with the TfR1 molecule, were selected for mutation. These mutations were designed to either form additional hydrogen bonds between HFn and TfR1 (F81Y, D123E, N109R and K119R) (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 1a) or enhance van der Waals interactions within the hydrophobic microenvironment (D15L and Q83H) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Relevant descriptions have been added to page 6 of the revised manuscript and are marked in red.
The structures of the HFn mutants were predicted via AlphaFold3 and superimposed onto the HFn molecule in the cryo-EM structure (PDB ID: 6H5I). The root-mean-square deviations (r.m.s.d.) in the positions of the carbon α atoms between the mutants and wtHFn ranged from 0.54 to 0.58 Å, indicating a high degree of structural similarity. In the N109R mutant, the amide group of R109 forms a hydrogen bond with the oxygen atom of E294 in TfR1, whereas in the K119R mutant, the amide group of R119 forms a hydrogen bond with the oxygen atom of Q197. The interaction interface and solvation free energy (ΔiG) gain upon interface formation, which is based on the HFn mutant–TfR1 complex structures, were predicted via PDBePISA software (Only for reviewer table 1). Unfortunately, we did not find any relationship between the solvation free energy gain upon formation of the interface (ΔiG) and the affinity obtained from the Biacore test, probably because the ΔiG value calculated with PDBePISA software does not include the effect of satisfactory hydrogen bonds and salt bridges across the interface, which is the mutation target in this experiment.
The predicted interface area between the HFn mutant and TfR1 seems to be consistent with the Biacore result. Compared with those of wtHFn, the interface areas between the two molecules of the complex increased in the HFn1, HFn2, HFn4 and HFn6 mutants and varied slightly in the HFn3 and HFn5 mutants. Those mutants whose interface area increased also achieved increased affinity in the Biacore test. HFn3 and HFn5, whose interface areas are comparable to that of wtHFn, have decreased affinities. We hypothesize that this phenomenon may be due to the inaccurate prediction of the structure by the Alpha Fold. Despite the enormous applications of alpha fold software in the field of structural prediction, its accuracy in predicting the protein flexible region still needs to be improved. Unfortunately, in our case, the HFn mutation sites lie in the flexible region. Experimental structure determination is time-consuming, and further computational prediction and computations based on a predicted structure are inaccurate. Therefore, we employed SPR technology to measure the actual affinity of the HFn mutants and TfR1 receptor to screen high-affinity proteins.
We sincerely appreciate the valuable suggestions made by the reviewers regarding the presentation of the figures. We have optimized the images and illustrations in the manuscript. The TfR1 molecule is shown in cyan, whereas wtHFn and its mutants as well as the related residues are presented in light blue and light brown, respectively. Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We have further elaborated on the results: treatment of cells with a caveolin-dependent endocytosis inhibitor (M-β-CD) or a macropinocytosis inhibitor (AMI) did not significantly affect HFn-LYTAC-mediated HER2 degradation, indicating that HFn-PEP does not enter cells via the caveolin-dependent HER2 endocytic or macropinocytic pathways (Fig. 4j).
To investigate the endocytic pathway involved in HER2 degradation mediated by the second mechanism, we constructed pFn-PEP , which does not interact with TfR1, and coincubated HER2 it with SKBR3 cells pretreated with various endocytosis inhibitors. The degradation of HER2 was then assessed. The results demonstrate that the second degradation mechanism also relies on clathrin-mediated endocytosis for the internalization and subsequent degradation of POI (Fig. 4l). In addition, both mechanisms require lysosomes for POI degradation (Fig. 4k, m).
To further investigate the contribution of the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism to HFn6-LYTAC-mediated POI degradation, confocal microscopy was employed to visualize and analyze the subcellular distribution of TfR1 during HER2 internalization mediated by HFn6- PEP . Following a 2- to 4-hour treatment of SKBR3 cells with HFn6-PEP , both HER2 HER2 HER2 and TfR1 internalization were clearly observed, and the internalized HER2 and TfR1 were significantly colocalized (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 5d). This finding indicates that under our experimental conditions, the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism plays a dominant role in the HER2 degradation process mediated by HFn6-PEP . However, when competitive HER2 inhibition was achieved with HFn6 or when pFn was used to prevent binding to TfR1, HFn-LYTAC retained a weak ability to degrade POI (Fig. 4e, g-i). Therefore, we propose that the two mechanisms through which HFn-LYTAC mediates POI degradation constitute a dynamic process: the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism plays a dominant role, and multivalent interaction-driven endocytosis is initiated only when HFn6 binding to TfR1 is blocked.

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. In the current publications, some TPDs are named according to lysosome-targeting receptors (e.g., TfR1—TransTAC; cytokine receptor—KineTAC), whereas others are designated based on their compositional elements (e.g., aptamer LYTAC for nucleic acid aptamers, Nano-LYTAC for polymeric nanomaterials, and peptide-based Pep-TAC). 1. The rationale for selecting the specific target residues (out of the listed candidates) to implement mutations to increase TfR1 binding affinity is not provided.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and suggestions. The selection of HFn mutation sites was based on the analysis of the structure of the HFn and TfR1 ectodomain complex. The N-terminal and BC loop regions of HFn interact with the apical domain of TfR1 (Fig. 2a, b). The structural reorganization caused by complex formation is limited to the side chains that are in direct contact with amino acids, resulting in a relatively low affinity between the two. Therefore, it is theoretically possible to increase the affinity of HFn for TfR1 by strengthening the interaction between the side chains of amino acids at the binding interface of HFn and TfR1 or by introducing more amino acid residues involved in the interaction. Consequently, residues D15, F81, Q83, N109, K119 and D123, which are located in the vicinity of the interaction region and have no or limited interactions with the TfR1 molecule, were selected for mutation. These mutations were designed to either form additional hydrogen bonds between HFn and TfR1 (F81Y, N109R, D123E, and K119R) (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 1a) or strengthen the van der Waals forces within the hydrophobic microenvironment (D15L and Q83H) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). Relevant discussions have been added to the revised manuscript and are marked in red:
“The affinity between HFn and the TfR1 ectodomain obtained via surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was in the range of 10–7 M (Supplementary Table 1), which was consistent with the affinity between HFn and TfR1 on the cell surface28. Among the HFn residues involved in common contacts (T5, Q14, D15, E17, A18, A19, N21, R22, N25, R79, F81, Q83, K86, K87, and E116) with TfR1, D15, F81, Q83, N109, K119 and D123 were selected for mutation to increase the affinity for TfR1. These residues, located in the vicinity of the interaction region (Fig. 2a, b), had no or limited interactions with the TfR1 molecule. Therefore, they were selected for mutation to form additional hydrogen bonds between HFn and TfR1 (F81Y, N109R, D123E, and K119R) (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 1a) or strengthen the van der Waals forces within the hydrophobic microenvironment (D15L and Q83H) (Supplementary Fig. 1a).”

8. The authors speculated cellular trafficking and multivalent interactions of HFn-LYTAC and POI as a mechanism of target protein degradation without convincing experimental validation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. In this study, we constructed wtHFn-LYTAC using wild-type HFn as a control to verify the necessity of building HFn mutants with high TfR1 affinity. In the degradation experiments of EGFR and PD-L1, we found that the degradation ability of HFn6-LYTAC was greater than that of wtHFn-LYTAC. In addition, affinity measurements revealed that owing to steric hindrance, wtHFn-Z and EGFR wtHFn-FN3 exhibited no TfR1 affinity but still retained weak POI degradation ability. PD-L1 Therefore, we propose that HFn-LYTAC involves a non-TfR1-dependent mechanism for degrading POI. Since HFn has nanoscale properties and multiple POI ligands are conjugated on its surface, we propose that the cellular trafficking of nanoparticles and the multivalent binding of POI to HFn-LYTAC constitute the second mechanism by which HFn-LYTAC mediates POI degradation.
To validate this, we chose ferritin derived from Pyrococcus furiosus (pFn) to conjugate with the POI ligand and constructed pFn-LYTAC to demonstrate the second degradation mechanism. The chosen PFn does not interact with human TfR1 but possesses a nanostructure similar to that of HFn. As anticipated, pFN-LYTAC was capable of mediating the degradation of HER2, EGFR, and PD-L1, although its degradation efficacy was lower than that of HFn6-LYTAC (Fig. 4g, h, i). These results indicate that HFn-LYTAC can degrade POI through cellular internalization and multivalent binding, with this non-TfR1-dependent mechanism exhibiting reduced degradation potency relative to the TfR1-dependent degradation pathway. Furthermore, we utilized pFn-LYTAC to investigate the endocytic pathway on which the second degradation mechanism relies. The results demonstrate that the second degradation mechanism also relies on clathrin-mediated endocytosis for the internalization and subsequent degradation of POI (Fig. 4l). These figures are shown in Question 9. The relevant content has been supplemented and revised in the revised manuscript:
“Recent studies have indicated that the cellular trafficking of nanoparticles can be leveraged to design TPD agents.……The endocytic pathways involved in the multivalent binding- mediated endocytic degradation mechanism have also been explored. reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In the revised version of the manuscript, the authors have addressed most of the issues raised in the first round of review. There are still several minor concerns need to be addressed.
(1) The biodistribution of the LYTAC in the major organs (such as liver, heart, spleen, lung, kidney, and brain) and tumor tissues (better in s.c. inoculated tumor models) should be determined.
(2) The serum half-life data shown in the rebuttal letter should be provided as the supplementary materials in the manuscript.
(3) The "x" shown in supp Table 1 and Table 2 should be corrected into multiplication sign.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors of this manuscript have made significant edits that improve the quality and clarity of the study. However, there are a few points raised in my prior review that could use additional improvement.
• Major comment 1 (The prose and figures frequently are mislabeled or unclear regarding POI removal from the cell surface (e.g., the flow method) versus degradation of POI (e.g., Western). These are both biologically meaningful but are quite different phenomena. This needs to be corrected and clear throughout the manuscript)
The authors have made significant edits that help clarify measurements between surface removal of target (e.g., flow cytometry of intact cells) versus total degradation of target (e.g., Western analysis of lysed cells). However, there are many instances in the prose of the manuscript as well as figure labels and legends where the removal of target from the surface of the cell is equated with degradation of the target.
When a surface receptor is endocytosed off the surface of the cell but is still intact and present in the endosome of the cell, it has not been degraded. It has only been removed from the cell surface. Unless experiments show that the surface-removed POI has in fact been degraded, it must not be described as degraded. It could be described as removed from the surface, surface depleted, or other phrasings, but not as degraded if it may still be a physically intact molecule that has been moved about within the cell.
Moreover, the authors identify this phenomenon themselves, e.g., p. 10 “These findings indicate that a portion of the EGFR on the cell membrane is internalized into the cell… but remains undegraded”. Yet while the y axis label for Fig 3b correctly describes the measurement as “relative surface EGFR”, the figure legend describes 3b as measuring the the “surface EGFR degradation” and the prose on page 9 and 10 describes it as degradation as well.
There are many locations within the manuscript where surface removal is equated with degradation, such as Fig 2e cartoon text, many figure legends, pages 8, 9 10, 14, and more.
Removal of the POI from the cell surface is a valuable biological phenomenon to measure, it just needs to not be mischaracterized.
I would ask the authors to thoroughly ensure that a protein is not described as “degraded” unless they have data showing it has been actually degraded versus potentially just endocytosed.
• Minor comment 5 (Figure legends/labels/descriptions need more details throughout)
The authors have added many details through the manuscript that are very helpful. There are a few more experimental details that should be provided if not present. This is important for ensuring interpretability and reproducibility of the work.
i. Fig. 4 g, h, i: timepoint?
ii. Fig. 6b: methods, time, concentration for transcytosis measurement?
iii. Supp. Fig. 2 o, p: how was membrane vs cytoplasmic protein determined?
iv. P. 9 (3 c) states there was not a statistically significant reduction of EGFR by ZEGFR or ferritin, but statistics are not provided comparing them to no treatment.
v. When y axes are labeled as “relative” (e.g., Fig 3, 4, Supp. Fig. 2, 3 4), it would be more clear to say what it is relative to; e.g., relative to no treatment.
• Minor comment 1 (300 nM of HFn-LYTAC is a high concentration)
The author’s addition on p. 28 is helpful, but should at least state that this dosage is equivalent on a MOLAR basis of the entire complex to 6 mg/kg IgG (if one were to calculate the molar equivalent amount of POI binders, it would be quite different).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: Most of the raised concerns are reasonably addressed. I have one recommendation. To enhance the reliability of the authors’ conclusion regarding comment #5, it would be ideal to selectively label intracellular EGFR, followed by quantitative analysis.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs) hold therapeutic potential by degrading pathogenesis-associated proteins. However, current LYTAC systems often require considerable effort for case-by-case construction and are devoid of a convenient and efficient modular platform. Here, we develop a modular LYTAC platform based on human heavy chain ferritin (HFn), leveraging its peptide-display function and TfR1-mediated lysosomal endocytosis. This system comprises a bioengineered HFn scaffold with enhanced TfR1 affinity and target-specific affibodies conjugated to the HFn via SpyTag-SpyCatcher system. Using this approach, HFn-LYTACs efficiently degrade epidermal growth factor receptor, epidermal growth factor receptor-2 and programmed death-ligand 1. Mechanistic studies indicate that the HFn-LYTAC platform mediates the degradation of POI via two distinct mechanisms: a TfR1-dependent endocytic pathway as well as the nanoparticle size and multivalent ligand effect of HFn-LYTAC. In vivo, HFn-LYTACs inhibit tumor growth with favorable safety. Therefore, the modular HFn-LYTAC platform represents a versatile, efficient, and promising strategy for tumor-targeted therapy.

---

## Introduction

Targeted protein degradation (TPD) is becoming a promising therapeutic strategy. In contrast to the "occupancy-driven" pharmacological paradigm of traditional blocking drugs, TPDs employ the intrinsic protein degradation pathway of cells to achieve the degradation of disease-causing proteins through simple binding for therapeutic purposes1-5. Therefore, TPD technology is anticipated to facilitate the identification of "undruggable" molecules that are challenging to use with conventional small-molecule drugs2,6.

There are two primary categories of protein degradation pathways utilized: proteasome-dependent TPD and lysosomal-dependent TPD. Proteasome-dependent TPDs, such as proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs)7, molecular glues8 and proteolysis-targeting antibodies (PROTABs)9, recruit E3 ligases to promote the ubiquitination of target proteins for degradation via the ubiquitin–proteasome system. These degraders efficiently degrade pathogenic proteins, and many are being tested in clinical trials10. However, the reliance on specific E3 ligase subunits not only limits the application of these degraders to particular cell types but also may lead to resistance in cancer cells following chronic treatment11.

Recently, the emergence of lysosome-dependent TPD agents, including lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs)12, autophagy-targeting chimeras (AUTACs)13 and autophagosome-tethering compounds (ATTECs)14, has further expanded the range of potential TPD targets by eliminating proteasome dependence. AUTACs and ATTECs facilitate the degradation of intracellular proteins or even damaged organelles via the autophagy pathway. LYTACs employ lysosomal-trafficking receptors to facilitate the degradation of both membrane proteins and extracellular proteins. Considering that the majority of drug targets are located at the cell surface or secreted, LYTACs are attracting increasing interest from scientists. A variety of antibody-based LYTACs12,15-18 or principally analogous LYTAC degraders19,20 have been developed. However, the preparation of antibody-based LYTACs generally requires sophisticated antibody engineering methodologies. Notably, LYTACs based on DNA aptamers or peptides have been developed and are capable of POI degradation. However, these degraders have limitations in terms of tissue persistence and require additional delivery systems for assistance21. Furthermore, the binding stability of short peptides is limited, and their performance needs to be enhanced through additional chemical modifications22. These factors restrict the construction and development of modular LYTAC systems. Therefore, it is imperative to develop a modular and easily constructed LYTAC platform.

Ferritin is a nanocage-like protein comprising 24 subunits and is widely expressed in humans. Human heavy chain ferritin (HFn) has been developed as a peptide display platform and nanodrug carrier for nanovaccine development and tumor therapy. HFn is capable of multivalent binding to the transferrin receptor (TfR1) and is subsequently endocytosed into lysosomes23. TfR1 is widely overexpressed in tumor cells and has been identified as a lysosomal-targeting receptor for developing TPD agents20,21,24,25. However, the binding of HFn to TfR1 and its subsequent internalization exhibit a threshold effect26 (Supplementary Fig. 4e, f), with HFn preferentially endocytosed by cells highly expressing TfR1, thereby ensuring the safety profile of HFn-LYTAC. Therefore, HFn is an ideal candidate for the construction of LYTACs.

Here, we designed a modular HFn-based LYTAC (HFn-LYTAC) platform for tumor therapy (Fig. 1). First, through structure-guided bioengineering, a HFn mutant with high affinity for TfR1 was screened, which serves as a universal modular nanoscaffold for LYTAC construction. With the SpyTag-SpyCatcher system, HFn-LYTACs were constructed via simple incubation to conjugate affibodies of POI to the surface of the HFn nanoscaffold. To validate the efficacy of the platform, we engineered HFn-LYTACs against three targets, including epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2), and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1). All HFn-LYTACs effectively degraded the corresponding proteins, with degradation efficiencies exceeding 60%, and some even approaching 80% (determined via Western blotting). Mechanistic investigations indicate that HFn-LYTAC mediates the degradation of POI through two distinct mechanisms. The first mechanism involves the formation of a ternary complex among HFn-LYTAC, TfR1 and POI, leading to subsequent endocytosis and degradation of POI in lysosomes. The second mechanism involves the cellular trafficking of nanoparticles (HFn nanocages), as well as the multivalent interaction between HFn-LYTAC and POI, which promotes direct endocytosis and degradation. The second mechanism is independent of TfR1. Therapeutic experiments conducted in subcutaneous xenograft mice indicated that HFn-LYTAC effectively inhibited tumor progression and maintained favorable safety. In addition, our previous work demonstrated that HFn is able to traverse the blood‒brain barrier (BBB)23, which enables HFn-LYTAC to be a viable option in the treatment of glioblastoma. Therefore, the HFn-LYTAC platform is a powerful TPD tool for tumor membrane protein degradation. As a modular platform, the flexibility and superior safety of LYTAC facilitate its broader application in the medical field.

---

## Results

Construction of HFn-LYTACs for EGFR degradation

First, the affinity of HFn for TfR1 was increased to acquire a modular scaffold for LYTAC construction. The complex structure of the HFn and TfR1 ectodomain from the cryoelectron microscopy data indicates that the N-terminal and BC loop regions of HFn interact with the apical domain of TfR127 (Fig. 2a, b). The structural reorganization induced by complex formation is constrained to the amino acid side chains in direct contact, leading to a diminished affinity between the two. Therefore, a series of HFn mutants were initially designed to increase their affinity for TfR1. The affinity between HFn and the TfR1 ectodomain obtained via surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was in the range of 10–7 M (Supplementary Table 1), which was consistent with the affinity between HFn and TfR1 on the cell surface28. Among the HFn residues involved in common contacts (T5, Q14, D15, E17, A18, A19, N21, R22, N25, R79, F81, Q83, K86, K87, and E116) with TfR1, D15, F81, Q83, N109, K119 and D123 were selected for mutation to increase the affinity for TfR1. These residues, located in the vicinity of the interaction region (Fig. 2a, b), had no or limited interactions with the TfR1 molecule. Therefore, they were selected for mutation to form additional hydrogen bonds between HFn and TfR1 (F81Y, N109R, D123E, and K119R) (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Fig. 1a) or strengthen the van der Waals forces within the hydrophobic microenvironment (D15L and Q83H) (Supplementary Fig. 1a). The wtHFn and HFn mutants were expressed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) and purified by hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC) and size exclusion chromatography (SEC). The affinity of the wtHFn and HFn mutants for TfR1 was subsequently determined via SPR (Supplementary Table 1). Among the mutants, variants HFn1 (D15L), HFn2 (F81Y) and HFn4 (N109R) exhibited enhanced affinity for TfR1, demonstrating a 2- to 5-fold increase compared with wtHFn. HFn6, an N109R/K119R mutant that presented a further increased affinity for TfR1 in the SPR experiment, exhibited a significantly reduced dissociation rate (koff), indicating a longer residence time on TfR1 (Fig. 2c).

Consequently, the HFn6 mutant was selected as the nanoscaffold for the development of HFn-LYTAC. The monomer of wtHFn comprises four α-helices (A-D helices) and one short E helix. The E-helix is located at the C-terminus and, following the self-assembly of a 24-mer HFn, is oriented toward the interior of the nanocage29. To mitigate the impact of the conjugated affibodies on the binding of HFn and TfR1, the SpyTag sequence was fused to the C-terminus of the HFn truncate with the E helix removed (Fig. 2d). The SPR results indicated that the fusion of the SpyTag sequence at the C-terminus of the HFn6-truncated variant (HFn6SpyTag) had a relatively modest effect on its affinity for TfR1 (Supplementary Table 1). The wtHFn truncated variant fused with the SpyTag sequence (wtHFnSpyTag) was also designed as a control.

Next, to demonstrate proof of concept, EGFR was chosen as a target protein to verify whether the HFn-LYTAC platform mediates membrane protein degradation. Affibodies against EGFR were obtained from previous studies30 and termed ZEGFR. A linker followed by the SpyCatcher domain was introduced to the C-terminus of ZEGFR for the construction of HFn-LYTAC, and a His tag was C-terminally fused to the SpyCatcher domain for purification (Fig. 2d).

Since HFn is a nanocage-like protein comprising 24 subunits, a single HFn nanocage is theoretically capable of coupling 24 binding affibodies. Consequently, we examined the influence of the conjugation ratio on EGFR degradation to develop HFn-LYTAC with optimal degradation efficiency (Fig. 2e). Specifically, HFn6SpyTag and ZEGFR-SpyCatcher were incubated at various molar ratios (ZEGFR-SpyCatcher: HFn6SpyTag ranging from 3:1 to 24:1) at room temperature for conjugation (HFn6-ZEGFR). The conjugation reaction was monitored by sodium dodecyl sulfate‒polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS‒PAGE) (Supplementary Fig. 1b). The ZEGFR-conjugated HFn6 monomer has a relatively high molecular weight, corresponding to the band with a molecular weight of approximately 40 kDa, as observed in the SDS‒PAGE image. Notably, no ZEGFR-SpyCatcher bands were observed at ZEGFR-SpyCatcher to HFn6SpyTag incubation ratios of less than 12:1, indicating complete conjugation of all the ZEGFRs to HFn6. As the incubation ratio increased, the intensity of the ZEGFR-SpyCatcher bands progressively intensified, suggesting a constrained additional coupling capacity of HFn6, potentially due to steric hindrance. Next, the EGFR degradation capacity of HFn6-ZEGFR at various incubation ratios was evaluated. U-87 MG cells, a glioblastoma cell line with high expression of both EGFR and TfR1, were incubated separately with different HFn6-ZEGFR samples for 24 hours, after which the surface levels of EGFR were quantified via flow cytometry. As the incubation ratio of ZEGFR-SpyCatcher and HFn6SpyTag increased, the clearance of surface EGFR on U-87 MG cells initially increased and subsequently decreased (Fig. 2f). HFn-LYTAC demonstrated optimal efficacy in surface EGFR clearance at ZEGFR : HFn6 incubation ratios of 12:1 and 15:1. This is because an increase in the number of ZEGFR molecules coupled to HFn enhances the chance of HFn-ZEGFR binding to EGFR on the cell surface, thereby improving its capacity to mediate clearance of surface EGFR. However, further elevation of the ZEGFR incubation ratio introduces steric hindrance, which could interfere with the interaction between HFn6 and TfR1. Moreover, at high ZEGFR incubation ratios, free ZEGFR in solution competitively inhibits HFn6-ZEGFR. Consequently, as the ZEGFR incubation ratio increases further, the clearance efficiency of HFn-ZEGFR toward surface EGFR gradually decreases. This specific conjugation ratio (ZEGFR : HFn6 = 12:1) was employed in subsequent experiments for EGFR degradation. We also fabricated ZEGFR-conjugated wtHFn (wtHFn-ZEGFR) at a molar ratio of 12:1 as a control. The constructed HFn6-ZEGFR and wtHFn-ZEGFR were characterized via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and dynamic light scattering (DLS). Both wtHFn and HFn6 exhibited a uniform spherical morphology, whereas HFn6-ZEGFR and wtHFn-ZEGFR displayed spherical shapes with irregular protrusions (Supplementary Fig. 1f, g, h). The hydrodynamic sizes of both HFn6-ZEGFR and wtHFn-ZEGFR were greater than those of the ZEGFR-unconjugated form. These data indicate that ZEGFR was successfully conjugated to the surface of the HFn nanoscaffold.

Following the identification of the optimal coupling ratio, the HFn6-ZEGFR-mediated degradation of EGFR in different cell lines was thoroughly evaluated (Fig. 3a). U-87 MG and MDA-MB-231 cells were treated with HFn6-ZEGFR for 24 h, and the surface levels of EGFR were measured via flow cytometry with an orthogonal detection antibody. In U-87 MG and MDA-MB-231 cells, the surface EGFR levels were significantly reduced by an average of 61% and 75%, respectively (Fig. 3b, c). Equivalent doses of ZEGFR or ferritin (wtHFn and HFn6) resulted in only a minor reduction in cell surface EGFR levels (<15% in U-87 MG cells and <20% in MDA-MB-231 cells). However, wtHFn-ZEGFR also demonstrated comparable efficacy in the clearance of surface EGFR. Total EGFR degradation was further evaluated by Western blotting. In U-87 MG cells, treatment with HFn6-ZEGFR resulted in 62% degradation of total EGFR (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 2a), which aligns with observations from cell surface clearance studies. In contrast, wtHFn-ZEGFR induced only 35% degradation of total EGFR, which does not correspond with the findings of cell surface clearance. In MDA-MB-231 cells, HFn6-ZEGFR and wtHFn-ZEGFR caused 65% and 57% degradation of total EGFR, respectively. (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig. 2b). To investigate the reasons for the discrepancy between the results of cell surface EGFR clearance and total EGFR degradation in U-87 MG cells mediated by wtHFn-ZEGFR, confocal microscopy was used to visualize EGFR degradation (Fig. 3f, g and Supplementary Fig. 2n). After treatment with HFn6-ZEGFR or wtHFn-ZEGFR for 24 h, the cytoplasmic EGFR signal in the wtHFn-ZEGFR treatment group was 50% stronger than that in the HFn6-ZEGFR group (Supplementary Fig. 2o). However, the membrane EGFR signals in U-87 MG cells were reduced in both treatment groups (Supplementary Fig. 2p). Cytoplasmic proteins were isolated from U-87 MG cells treated with HFn-LYTAC using a membrane and cytosol protein extraction kit (Beyotime), and the expression levels of EGFR in the cytoplasm were analyzed by Western blotting. The results consistently exhibited higher EGFR levels in the wtHFn-ZEGFR treatment group compared to the HFn6-ZEGFR group (Supplementary Fig. 2q). These findings indicate that a portion of the EGFR on the cell membrane is internalized into the cell following its binding to wtHFn-ZEGFR but remains undegraded. This phenomenon will be further discussed in subsequent chapters. In addition, previous studies have reported that EGFR degradation results in reduced levels of p-AKT in its downstream signaling pathway31. This effect was confirmed following the treatment of U-87 MG cells with HFn6-ZEGFR. Owing to differences in total EGFR degradation capacity, the level of p-AKT in U-87 MG cells treated with wtHFn-ZEGFR was slightly greater than that in those treated with HFn6-ZEGFR (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Therefore, there is also a difference in their ability to inhibit cell proliferation. The IC50 value of HFn6-ZEGFR in U-87 MG cells was 24.2 nM, which was less than half that of wtHFn-ZEGFR (57.26 nM). Equivalent doses of HFn6 or ZEGFR did not demonstrate cytotoxic effects.(Supplementary Fig. 3b, c).

Expanding the target scope of the HFn-LYTAC

To explore the capacity of the HFn-LYTAC platform to degrade additional membrane targets, HER2 and PD-L1 were selected as the target proteins. The affibodies against HER2 and PD-L1 were derived from previous studies32,33 and termed PEPHER2 and FN3PD-L1, respectively. The protein sequence design of PEPHER2-Spycatcher and FN3PD-L1-Spycatcher for the construction of HFn-LYTAC was similar to that of ZEGFR-Spycatcher. The conjugation ratio of PEPHER2 and FN3PD-L1 to HFn6 was subsequently optimized. Similarly, owing to steric hindrance, HFn6 cannot conjugate with 24 affibodies (Supplementary Fig. 1c, d). The clearance of surface HER2 or PD-L1 by different incubation ratios of HFn-LYTAC exhibited a similar pattern to that of HFn6-ZEGFR (Fig. 2g, h). HFn-LYTAC demonstrated optimal surface HER2 clearance efficacy at a PEPHER2 to HFn6 conjugation ratio of 12:1. For PD-L1 target degradation, The optimal clearance efficiency of surface PD-L1 was achieved when FN3PD-L1 was conjugated with HFn6 at a ratio of 6:1. This may be because FN3PD-L1 has a relatively high molecular weight, thereby leading to enhanced steric hindrance effects. HFn6-PEPHER2 with a conjugation ratio of 12:1 and HFn6-FN3PD-L1 with a conjugation ratio of 6:1 were utilized for the following experiments. HFn6-PEPHER2 and HFn6-FN3PD-L1 were characterized via DLS and TEM (Supplementary Fig. 1f, h). Both HFn6-PEPHER2 and HFn6-FN3PD-L1 exhibited good dispersibility. Notably, HFn6-FN3PD-L1 has a relatively large hydrodynamic diameter, which is attributed to the largest molecular weight of the FN3PD-L1 ligand (Supplementary Fig. 1e). This observation suggests that, compared with other ligands, FN3PD-L1 has a more pronounced steric hindrance effect.

Furthermore, the HFn6-LYTAC-mediated degradation of HER2 and PD-L1 in different cell lines was evaluated (Fig. 3h, o). To substantiate the rationale for constructing the HFn6 mutant, we synthesized wtHFn-LYTAC as a control. For HER2 target degradation, SKBR3 and NCI-N87 cells were treated with HFn6-PEPHER2 for 24 h, after which the surface and total HER2 protein levels were quantified via flow cytometry and Western blotting, respectively. In SKBR3 and NCI-N87 cells, the levels of membrane HER2 decreased by more than 70%. (Fig. 3i, j), whereas the average degradation rates of total HER2 were 77% for SKBR3 cells and 63% for NCI-N87 cells (Fig. 3k, l and Supplementary Fig. 2c, d). Treatment with equivalent doses of PEPHER2 did not lead to a reduction in HER2 levels on the cell membrane or in the whole cell. However, no significant difference in HER2 degradation was observed between HFn6-PEPHER2 and wtHFn-PEPHER2, regardless of whether membrane HER2 or total HER2 was assessed. Confocal microscopy visualization of HER2 following treatment with HFn6-PEPHER2 or wtHFn-PEPHER2 revealed reduced HER2 signals, which was consistent with the findings from flow cytometry and Western blotting (Fig. 3m, n). The cytotoxic effects of HFn6-PEPHER2 and wtHFn-PEPHER2 were evaluated in SKBR3 cells. Neither HFn6 nor PEPHER2 demonstrated cytotoxicity, but both HFn6-PEPHER2 and wtHFn-PEPHER2 effectively inhibited the proliferation of SKBR3 cells. Given that they have the same HER2 degradation capacity, their IC50 values for SKBR3 cells are similar (Supplementary Fig. 3d, e). The IC50 of HFn6-PEPHER2 was 6.78 nM, and that of wtHFn-PEPHER2 was 9.29 nM. Moreover, HT1080 and MDA-MB-231 cells were used to evaluate the degradation of PD-L1 mediated by HFn6-FN3PD-L1 and wtHFn-FN3PD-L1. The average reduction rate of surface PD-L1 mediated by HFn6-FN3PD-L1 in both cell lines was approximately 50%, which was significantly higher than the 35% reduction rate mediated by wtHFn-FN3PD-L1 (Fig. 3p, q). The average degradation rates of total PD-L1 mediated by HFn6-FN3PD-L1 were greater than 65% for HT1080 cells and 60% for MDA-MB-231 cells, which were greater than those mediated by wtHFn-FN3PD-L1 (Fig. 3r, s and Supplementary Fig. 2e, f). Confocal microscopy visualization of PD-L1 following treatment with HFn6-FN3PD-L1 or wtHFn-FN3PD-L1 was consistent with the flow cytometry and Western blotting results (Fig. 3t, u). The degradation of HER2 and PD-L1 yielded distinct conclusions, whereas the degradation of PD-L1 mediated by HFn6-FN3PD-L1 was markedly greater than that mediated by wtHFn-FN3PD-L1, whereas there was no significant difference in the degradation of HER2 mediated by HFn6-PEPHER2 and wtHFn-PEPHER2. This phenomenon will be further investigated in mechanistic studies. Notably, the HFn-LYTACs developed in this study for three POIs did not lead to a decrease in total intracellular TfR1 levels (Supplementary Fig. 2g-l), which was attributed to the ability of TfR1 to be recycled back to the cell membrane34. Overall, these results for three different targets demonstrate the universality of the HFn-LYTAC platform for degrading cell-surface proteins (Supplementary Fig. 2m).

Principles and mechanisms of HFn-LYTAC-mediated target degradation

HER2 was selected as the model target to investigate the principles and mechanisms underlying protein degradation mediated by HFn-LYTAC. HFn6-PEPHER2 mediated over 50% degradation of HER2 following a 24-hour treatment. Within 24–48 hours after treatment with HFn6-PEPHER2, the total HER2 level in the SKBR3 cells remained low (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Fig. 4a). The degradation of HER2 in SKBR3 cells was found to be concentration dependent, with the concentration of HFn6-PEPHER2 required to achieve 50% degradation of total HER2 calculated to be 102.9 nM (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Fig. 4b). The HER2 level was restored to approximately 70% at 48 hours after HFn6-PEPHER2 washout, suggesting that the degradation of HER2 by HFn6-PEPHER2 is reversible (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Next, confocal microscopy was employed to visualize the process by which HFn6-PEPHER2 mediates HER2 internalization (Fig. 4c, Supplementary Fig. 5a). Following a 2-hour treatment with HFn6-PEPHER2, HER2 signaling was observed in SKBR3 cells and colocalized with HFn6-PEPHER2, indicating that HFn6-PEPHER2 associated with HER2 and facilitated its internalization. A 4-hour treatment with HFn6-PEPHER2 resulted in significant HER2 internalization. Notably, the internalized HER2 signals colocalized with lysosome-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1), suggesting that HER2 is internalized into lysosomes for degradation (Supplementary Fig. 5b).

To investigate the role of TfR1 in the degradation of target proteins mediated by HFn-LYTAC, a TfR1-knockdown SKBR3 cell line was established (Supplementary Fig. 4d). After TfR1 knockdown, the reduction of surface HER2 induced by HFn6-PEPHER2 was significantly inhibited. However, in cells transfected with nontargeting shRNA, the reduction of surface HER2 remained unaffected. (Fig. 4d). Moreover, coincubation with HFn6 at fivefold greater concentrations also significantly inhibited the degradation of HER2 mediated by HFn6-PEPHER2 (Fig. 4e). These data indicate that HFn-LYTAC is dependent on TfR1. However, the knockdown of TfR1 or competitive inhibition of HFn6 did not completely abolish the degradation effect of HFn-LYTAC, as HFn6-PEPHER2 still degraded 30–40% of HER2. Recent studies have indicated that the cellular trafficking of nanoparticles can be leveraged to design TPD agents35. HFn is a nanocage-like protein with an outer diameter of 12 nm. Consequently, we propose that the cellular trafficking of nanoparticles (HFn nanocages) facilitates the internalization and subsequent degradation of HER2. To test this hypothesis, ferritin derived from Pyrococcus furiosus (pFn), which does not interact with human TfR1 but possesses a similar nanostructure, was chosen for conjugation with PEPHER2. As anticipated, treatment of SKBR3 cells with pFn-PEPHER2 for 24 h led to less than 40% degradation of total HER2, which was more than 20% lower than that of HFn6-PEPHER2 and wtHFn-PEPHER2 (Fig. 4g). Furthermore, pFn-ZEGFR and pFn-FN3PD-L1 were constructed to evaluate the generalizability of the hypothesis. Treatment of U-87 MG cells with pFn-ZEGFR for 24 h resulted in an average 40% degradation of total EGFR (Fig. 4h), and pFn-FN3PD-L1 mediated the degradation of an average of 30% of total PD-L1 in HT1080 cells (Fig. 4i). Furthermore, upon reviewing the experiments regarding the conjugation ratio between the affibody and HFn6, the surface PD-L1 clearance efficiency achieved with a 1:6 molar ratio of HFn6 to affibody was significantly higher than that observed with a 1:3 ratio. Consequently, the multivalent binding of HFn-LYTAC with POI can also enhance its degradation effect. We believe that the nanoparticle size effects of HFn-LYTAC (cellular trafficking of nanoparticles) and the multivalent binding to POI form a synergistic effect, jointly mediating the degradation of POI. Collectively, these findings demonstrated that HFn-LYTAC mediated the degradation of the POI through two complementary mechanisms. The first involves simultaneous binding to TfR1 and POI, thereby facilitating endocytosis of the POI via TfR1-dependent pathways, resulting in its subsequent degradation in lysosomes. The second mechanism involves cellular trafficking of the nanoparticles and multivalent interactions between HFn-LYTAC and POI, which promote direct endocytosis and degradation. The advantage of the second mechanism lies in its independence from lysosomal endocytosis receptors, thereby broadening the application scope of HFn-LYTAC. However, its degradation efficiency remains limited, which may partially restrict therapeutic efficacy, but contributes to ensuring biological safety. The degradation efficiency of the second mechanism may be influenced by the size of the nanoparticle and the quantity of conjugated affibody molecules.

Interestingly, the EGFR degradation efficiency mediated by wtHFn-ZEGFR was comparable to that mediated by pFn-ZEGFR, suggesting that wtHFn-ZEGFR relies primarily on the second mechanism for EGFR degradation. To investigate the factors affecting the two degradation mechanisms, the affinity of all HFn-LYTACs for POI and TfR1 was determined via SPR (Supplementary Table 2). Owing to the multivalent binding effect, the affinity of HFn-LYTAC for the corresponding target (POI) was greater than two orders of magnitude greater than that of the free affibody. However, the conjugation of ZEGFR and FN3PD-L1 resulted in a diminished affinity of HFn6 for TfR1. This was especially the case for the HFn-LYTAC constructed on the basis of wtHFn, where its affinity for TfR1 was completely abrogated. A diminished affinity for TfR1 results in a compromised TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism, consequently reducing the efficiency of POI degradation. The conjugation of PEPHER2 had minimal influence on the binding affinity of HFn to TfR1, thereby allowing the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism to remain functional. These data also indicate that when the affinity of HFn-LYTAC for TfR1 reaches 10–6 M, further increasing the affinity of HFn for TfR1 has a negligible effect on enhancing the degradation efficiency of HFn-LYTAC. Nevertheless, given the potential inhibitory effect of affibody conjugation on the affinity of HFn for TfR1, it is essential to design HFn mutants with enhanced affinity for TfR1.

To further investigate the contribution of the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism to HFn6-LYTAC-mediated POI degradation, confocal microscopy was employed to visualize and analyze the subcellular distribution of TfR1 during HER2 internalization mediated by HFn6-PEPHER2. Following a 2- to 4-hour treatment of SKBR3 cells with HFn6-PEPHER2, both HER2 and TfR1 internalization were clearly observed, and internalized HER2 and TfR1 were significantly colocalized (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Fig. 5c, d). These findings indicate that the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism plays a dominant role in the HER2 degradation process mediated by HFn6-PEPHER2. However, when competitive inhibition was achieved with HFn6 or when pFn was used to prevent binding to TfR1, HFn-LYTAC retained a weak ability to degrade POI (Fig. 4e, g-i). Therefore, the two mechanisms through which HFn-LYTAC mediates POI degradation constitute a dynamic process: the TfR1-dependent degradation mechanism plays a dominant role, and multivalent interaction-driven endocytosis is initiated only when HFn6 binding to TfR1 is blocked.

To investigate the internalization pathway of HFn6-LYTACS, chlorpromazine (CPZ), methyl-β-cyclodextrin (M-β-CD) or amiloride were utilized to inhibit clathrin- and caveolin-dependent endocytosis or micropinocytosis, respectively. In the CPZ pretreatment group, total HER2 degradation mediated by HFn6-PEPHER2 was significantly inhibited, whereas pretreatment with M-β-CD and amiloride had no effect on HER2 degradation. These findings indicate that HFn6-PEPHER2 is internalized into the cytoplasm via the clathrin-dependent endocytosis pathway (Fig. 4j). Pretreatment of SKBR3 cells with chloroquine inhibited the HFn6-PEPHER2-mediated degradation of HER2, confirming that the degradation promoted by LYTACs is dependent on lysosomes (Fig. 4k). The endocytic pathways involved in the multivalent binding-mediated endocytic degradation mechanism have also been explored. Inhibition of the clathrin-mediated endocytosis pathway by CPZ led to suppression of HER2 degradation mediated by pFn-PEPHER2, whereas pretreatment with M-β-CD and amiloride had no effect on HER2 degradation (Fig. 4l). Similarly, inhibition of lysosomal activity by chloroquine resulted in suppressed HER2 degradation mediated by HFn6-PEPHER2 (Fig. 4m).

In vivo antitumor efficacy and safety of the HFn-LYTAC platform

To evaluate the in vivo antitumor efficacy of HFn-LYTAC, HER2 was chosen as a model target, and the inhibitory effect of HFn6-PEPHER2 on the NCI-N87 xenograft tumor model was evaluated. The plasma half-life and tissue distribution of HFn6-PEPHER2 were first evaluated. Blood samples were collected at different time points following intravenous (i.v.) injection of Cy5.5-labeled HFn6-PEPHER2 or PEPHER2. Plasma was separated and the fluorescence intensity was detected. HFn6-PEPHER2 exhibited a prolonged circulation half-life of 131.8 min, which was more than tenfold longer than that of the PEPHER2 control group (9.3 min; Supplementary Fig. 7a). Given that the shedding of fluorescent groups could interfere with the accurate characterization of HFn6-PEPHER2, Western blotting was further utilized to directly evaluate its plasma half-life. The relative content of SpyCatcher in the plasma was detected and the plasma half-life of HFn6-PEPHER2 was determined to be 227 minutes (Fig. 5a). Tissue accumulation studies in the NCI-N87 xenograft mouse model demonstrated that 24 h after i.v. injection of HFn-PEPHER2, the average level of HFn6-PEPHER2 in tumors was over 5 times greater than that in the heart, spleen and lungs (Fig. 5b). The strong accumulation of HFn6-PEPHER2 in the liver and kidneys suggests that these organs are major sites of its metabolism. The low level of HFn6-PEPHER2 accumulation in the mouse brain indicates its capacity to cross the BBB. Given the nanoparticle properties of HFn6-PEPHER2, we investigated its uptake by monocytes and dendritic cells (Supplementary Fig. 6a). The uptake of HFn6 by SKBR3 cells was greater than that of HFn6-PEPHER2, a difference attributed to the dual-target binding mode of HFn6-PEPHER2. Compared with SKBR3 cells, DC2.4 cells had a slightly lower capacity for internalizing HFn6-PEPHER2. RAW 264.7 cells demonstrated robust endocytic activity toward both HFn6 and HFn6-PEPHER2, suggesting that a portion of HFn6-PEPHER2 may be taken up and cleared by monocytes following i.v. injection. Notably, the endocytosis of HFn6-PEPHER2 by RAW 264.7 cells and DC 2.4 cells did not significantly affect their proliferation (Supplementary Fig. 6b, c). Nevertheless, the multimerization of PEPHER2 displayed on HFn6 markedly enhances the binding affinity for HER2, enabling HFn6-PEPHER2 to rapidly engage HER2 after traversing the vasculature and reaching the tumor site, thereby facilitating detectable accumulation within the tumor (Fig. 5c). Compared with free PEPHER2, HFn6-PEPHER2 accumulated more persistently at the tumor site. This is attributed to the small molecular size of PEPHER2, which renders it susceptible to rapid clearance and degradation.

Next, the in vivo efficacy of HFn6-PEPHER2 in inhibiting tumor growth and its capacity to degrade POI were systematically evaluated (Fig. 5d). HFn6-PEPHER2 was administered at a dose of 30.6 mg/kg via the tail vein every 2 days. Owing to the large molecular weight of HFn-LYTACs (approximately 720 kDa on average), this dosage is equivalent to approximately 6 mg/kg of IgG (≈42 nmol/kg, on a molar basis of the entire HFn6-PEPHER2). After 7 administrations, tumor proliferation was significantly suppressed in the HFn6-PEPHER2 treatment group compared with the PBS control group (Fig. 5e, f). In contrast, equimolar doses of PEPHER2 and HFn6 exhibited no tumor suppressive activity. Two days after the final injection, the tumors were harvested, and HER2 levels in the tumor tissue were evaluated via flow cytometry and immunofluorescence. Significant HER2 degradation was observed in the HFn6-PEPHER2 treatment group (Fig. 5g, h). Furthermore, immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that HFn6-PEPHER2 treatment did not alter the expression level of TfR1 in tumor tissues. (Fig. 5i).

Furthermore, the long-term safety of HFn-PEPHER2 after administration was also evaluated. The endotoxin level of purified protein was measured to not exceed 10 EU/mg, remaining within acceptable limits (Supplementary Fig. 1i). No weight loss was observed during the treatment process (Supplementary Fig. 7d). Histopathological analysis of the major organs in NCI-N87 xenograft mice after HFn6-PEPHER2 administration revealed that these organs retained typical physiological morphology, with no significant pathological abnormalities or lesions detected, including those in the liver, where HFn6-PEPHER2 was highly enriched (Fig. 5j). Prussian blue staining of liver tissue sections revealed that it does not significantly alter iron deposition levels in liver tissue, indicating that HFn6-PEPHER2 does not affect hemosiderin content (Supplementary Fig. 7c). Serum biochemical analysis indicated that HFn6-PEPHER2 administration did not cause liver or kidney toxicity in mice (Fig. 5k, l). Considering the physiological functions of ferritin and the role of TfR1 in erythropoiesis36,37, complete blood count (CBC) analysis was performed following treatment of the mice. No differences were observed among the PBS-, PEPHER2-, HFn6- or HFn6-PEPHER2-treated groups in terms of red blood cell (RBC) counts or hemoglobin (HGB) levels (Fig. 5m). No significant difference in reticulocyte (RET) content was observed in the peripheral blood of mice across the different treatment groups (Supplementary Fig. 7b).

HFn-LYTAC platform for the treatment of glioblastoma

More than 60% of glioblastomas overexpress EGFR, which promotes tumor growth, survival, angiogenesis, and invasion38. However, the presence of the BBB hinders the clinical efficacy of small molecule inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies that target EGFR39,40. Our previous work demonstrated that HFn can traverse the BBB23, making HFn-LYTAC a promising candidate for glioblastoma therapy. Consequently, the inhibitory effect of HFn6-ZEGFR on the U-87 MG orthotopic xenograft tumor mouse model was evaluated. To investigate the ability of HFn6-ZEGFR to cross the BBB, a transcytosis assay was performed using mouse brain endothelial cells. Both HFn6 and HFn6-ZEGFR effectively traverse the mouse BBB, and the transport rate is 3-fold greater than that of human light chain ferritin (LFn) (Fig. 6a, b). Moreover, an orthotopic xenograft mouse model of tumors was established using U-87 MG cells expressing luciferase. Fluorescence imaging of the brains of U-87 MG orthotopic xenograft mice demonstrated that HFn6-ZEGFR successfully traversed the mouse BBB and accumulated in glioblastoma. Although the establishment of orthotopic xenograft mice may partially compromise the integrity of the BBB, the accumulation of HFn6-ZEGFR in glioblastoma was more than twice that of ZEGFR 1 h after i.v. injection, suggesting that HFn6-ZEGFR possesses the ability to cross the BBB and specifically target brain tumors(Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 7e). Next, the in vivo efficacy of HFn6-ZEGFR in inhibiting glioblastoma growth and its capacity to degrade POI were evaluated (Fig. 6d). HFn6-ZEGFR was intravenously injected at a dose of 10 mg/kg every two days. No weight loss was observed during the treatment process (Supplementary Fig. 7f). After seven administrations, tumor proliferation was significantly inhibited in the HFn6-ZEGFR treatment group compared with the PBS control group (Fig. 6e, f). In contrast, neither ZEGFR nor HFn6 demonstrated any tumor-suppressive activity. Two days after the final injection, the tumors were harvested for detection of EGFR degradation. Flow cytometry of tumor cells and immunofluorescence of tumor tissue revealed that EGFR was significantly degraded in the HFn6-ZEGFR treatment group (Fig. 6g, h). In the tumor tissue samples, the expression levels of TfR1 were not significantly different among the different treatment groups (Fig. 6h). In summary, these data indicate that the HFn-LYTAC platform has significant antitumor activity and good safety. Therefore, it is considered a promising drug for tumor treatment.

On the basis of the ability of HFn to target TfR1 and the advantages of peptide display platforms, we developed a modular targeted degradation platform capable of effectively degrading different membrane proteins on various tumor cell types. On the one hand, HFn-LYTAC facilitates the internalization of POI into lysosomes for degradation by concurrently recruiting TfR1 and POI. On the other hand, the cellular trafficking of the nanoparticles and the multivalent interaction of HFn-LYTAC with POI also promoted their internalization and degradation. In addition, enhancing the affinity of HFn for TfR1 facilitates the promotion of the TfR1-dependent degradation pathway, thereby increasing the efficiency of HFn-LYTAC in degrading POI. Considering the extensive high expression of TfR1 in tumor cells, HFn-LYTAC has significant potential for cancer therapy. Our findings provide preliminary evidence that HFn-LYTAC has antitumor activity and favorable safety.

A notable advantage of HFn-LYTAC lies in its modularity, making the construction process easy and straightforward. Two components, the TfR1 affinity-optimized HFn nanoscaffold and affibody of POI, can be easily obtained through prokaryotic expression and purification. The high stability and robust heat resistance of HFn render it particularly advantageous for purification and storage. By employing the SpyTag-SpyCatcher system, HFn-LYTACs targeting different POIs can be constructed by simply incubating the HFn nanoscaffold with the corresponding affibodies. In addition, HFn serves as an excellent nanomedicine carrier, facilitating the implementation of combination therapy for cancer. The ability of HFn to traverse the BBB makes HFn-LYTAC a viable option for the treatment of glioblastoma. The endocytosis of HFn is subjected to a threshold effect of TfR1 expression, thereby making it safer than antibodies. Overall, the HFn-LYTAC platform represents a promising approach for the targeted degradation of membrane proteins. Its efficient degradation capability, modular design, straightforward construction, and tumor-targeting potential support its broad applicability in cancer therapy and other biological fields.
